summary.title: Git's database internals I: packed object store
summary.one_liner: You learn how Git stores objects in the .git/objects store and compresses them into packfiles using pack-indexes, delta compression, and repacking.
keywords: why git does not use b-trees
how does git store data on disk
takeaways: Git's object store is a content-addressable store where objects (blobs, trees, commits, tags) are keyed by the hash of their contents.
Packfiles store objects compressed individually and against each other using offset deltas, while pack-index files enable fast binary-search lookups by object ID.
Tree objects change in small ways between commits, so delta compression stores them very compactly; this is why large binary files compress poorly in Git.
Delta chains trade a bit of read-time CPU for smaller storage; git pack.depth defaults to a limit of 50.
Git avoids B-trees because packfiles and indexes are static once written; repacking is done via git repack, git gc, geometric repack, or incremental maintenance.
summary.summary: The article is the first part of a five-part series on Git internals, framing Git as a distributed database and explaining its object model (blobs, trees, commits, tags) and reference store. It shows commands such as git cat-file, git hash-object and git log to query the object store. The main focus is packfiles: how pack and multi-pack indexes speed lookups, how delta compression exploits similarity between versions (especially tree objects), and the trade-offs of delta chain length. It closes with repacking strategies (git repack, geometric repack, incremental maintenance) and why Git does not use B-trees.
